title: Add Address embeddable and capture the flattened DDL
description: Define an Address embeddable (street, city, country — all strings) and embed it on Author in inline mode (the default). Add a typed metadata jsonb column to Article using p.json<ArticleMetadata>() where ArticleMetadata has readTimeMinutes: number and featuredImageUrl: string | null. Add a beforeCreate hook on Article that auto-generates slug from title (lowercase, replace spaces with hyphens, strip non-alphanumeric). Run 'npx mikro-orm schema:update --dump' and submit a screenshot of the 'create table author' portion — it must show four address_* columns inlined into the author table (address_street, address_city, address_country), proving the embeddable was flattened rather than stored in a separate table.
modelAnswer:
The screenshot must show author table columns including: address_street varchar not null, address_city varchar not null, address_country varchar not null — all directly in the author table, not in a separate address table.
If you see a CREATE TABLE address: you used the entity decorator instead of embeddable. The @Embeddable() decorator (or defineEntity with embeddable: true) is required.
If address columns are missing entirely: the embeddable was not registered in the entity's defineEntity block. Confirm the embedded property is present with p.embedded(() => Address).

title: JSONB concurrent counter danger + L6/L7 callback
description:
This task combines embeddables and JSONB (L8) with filters and migrations from L6–L7.

Part A (L8): In 4–6 sentences explain why storing an integer counter inside a JSONB column is dangerous under concurrent writes, while putting the same counter in a plain int column is safe. Reference how Postgres updates JSONB internally (whole-field rewrite) and why that causes lost-update under read-modify-write.

Part B (L6–L7 callback): You decide to extract the counter from JSONB into a dedicated view_count int column. Write the migration up() method in pseudocode or real TypeScript (using this.addColumn and this.addSql) that: (1) adds the view_count column with default 0, (2) backfills it from the JSONB field (you can use raw SQL), and (3) drops the JSONB key. Also: what filter (from L6) would you need to update or re-test after this migration?

Submit both parts as text.

title: Implement MoneyType custom type — plan, build, critique (AI-resilient)
description:
Implement a custom MikroORM Type called MoneyType that stores a Money value object (amount: number, currency: string) as 'amount:currency' string in Postgres. It must implement convertToDatabaseValue (object→string) and convertToJSValue (string→object). Apply it to a price property on Book.

Three-stage task:
1. Plan: before coding, identify the four methods a custom Type must implement and what each does. Write them as stubs with just their signatures and a one-line comment.
2. Implement: build MoneyType, apply it to Book.price, run schema:update --dump, confirm the price column is stored as varchar. Create a Book with a price, flush, reload it, and verify the JS value is a Money object (not a raw string).
3. Critique: paste your MoneyType into ChatGPT and ask 'What edge cases does this miss?' Copy the response. Write 3 sentences on what ChatGPT got right and what it missed specifically about the MikroORM Type contract (e.g., getColumnType(), compareAsType()).

Metacognitive memo: What does building a custom Type clarify about how MikroORM's mapping layer works that reading the docs alone does not?

title: Why is storing a counter in JSONB a concurrency trap, not just a style choice?
description: Two concurrent HTTP requests each want to increment article.metadata.viewCount by 1. Walk through the exact sequence of operations — read, modify, write — for both requests under optimistic (no row lock) conditions and explain why the final count is 1 instead of 2. Then explain why the same two requests incrementing a plain int view_count column with UPDATE article SET view_count = view_count + 1 WHERE id = $1 do produce a final count of 2. Your answer should reference Postgres row-level locking. Answer in 5–7 sentences.
